entries.17177063e37b01fa454fb18409faccb7bce3a776: <div sID="gen17300" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="6" osisID="Jer.6" sID="Jer.6"/> <div eID="gen17300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17301" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17302" type="x-p"/> In this chapter, as before, we have, I. A prophecy of the invading of the land of Judah and the besieging of Jerusalem by the Chaldean army (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.1-Jer.6.6">ver. 1-6</reference>), with the spoils they should make of the country (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.9">ver. 9</reference>) and the terror which all should be seized with on that occasion, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.22-Jer.6.26">ver. 22-26</reference>. II. An account of those sins of Judah and Jerusalem which provoked God to bring this desolating judgment upon them. Their oppression (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.7">ver. 7</reference>), their contempt of the word of God (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.10-Jer.6.12">ver. 10-12</reference>), their worldliness (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.13">ver. 13</reference>), the treachery of their prophets (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.14">ver. 14</reference>), their impudence in sin (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.15">ver. 15</reference>), their obstinacy against reproofs (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.18-Jer.6.19">ver. 18, 19</reference>), which made their sacrifices unacceptable to him (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.20">ver. 20</reference>), and for which he gave them up to ruin (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.21">ver. 21</reference>), but tried them first (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.27">ver. 27</reference>) and then rejected them as irreclaimable, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.28-Jer.6.30">ver. 28-30</reference>. III. Good counsel given them in the midst of all this, but in vain, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.8">ver. 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.16">16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.17">17</reference>.
entries.21722aef01d17ca781c88a0555a48d339a2349bb: <div eID="gen17302" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17301" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Judgments Threatened against Israel; The Doom of Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 608.)</title> <div sID="gen17303" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> O ye children of Benjamin, gather yourselves to flee out of the midst of Jerusalem, and blow the trumpet in Tekoa, and set up a sign of fire in Beth-haccerem: for evil appeareth out of the north, and great destruction. <hi type="super">2</hi> I have likened the daughter of Zion to a comely and delicate <hi type="italic">woman.</hi> <hi type="super">3</hi> The shepherds with their flocks shall come unto her; they shall pitch <hi type="italic">their</hi> tents against her round about; they shall feed every one in his place. <hi type="super">4</hi> Prepare ye war against her; arise, and let us go up at noon. Woe unto us! for the day goeth away, for the shadows of the evening are stretched out. <hi type="super">5</hi> Arise, and let us go by night, and let us destroy her palaces. <hi type="super">6</hi> For thus hath the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts said, Hew ye down trees, and cast a mount against Jerusalem: this <hi type="italic">is</hi> the city to be visited; she <hi type="italic">is</hi> wholly oppression in the midst of her. <hi type="super">7</hi> As a fountain casteth out her waters, so she casteth out her wickedness: violence and spoil is heard in her; before me continually <hi type="italic">is</hi> grief and wounds. <hi type="super">8</hi> Be thou instructed, O Jerusalem, lest my soul depart from thee; lest I make thee desolate, a land not inhabited. <div eID="gen17303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17304" type="x-p"/> Here is I. Judgment threatened against Judah and Jerusalem. The city and the country were at this time secure and under no apprehension of danger; they saw no cloud gathering, but every thing looked safe and serene: but the prophet tells them that they shall shortly be invaded by a foreign power, an army shall be brought against them <hi type="italic">from the north,</hi> which shall lay all waste, and shall cause not only a general consternation, but a general desolation. It is here foretold, <div eID="gen17304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17305" type="x-p"/> 1. That the alarm of this should be loud and terrible. This is represented, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.1">v. 1</reference>. The children of Benjamin, in which tribe part of Jerusalem lay, are here called to shift for their own safety in the country; for the city (to which it was first thought advisable for them to flee, <reference osisRef="Jer.4.5-Jer.4.6">ch. iv. 5, 6</reference>) would soon be made too hot for them, and they would find it the wisest course to flee out of the midst of it. It is common, in public frights, for the people to think any place safer than that in which they are; and therefore those in the city are for shifting into the country, in hopes there to escape out of danger, and those in the country are for shifting into the city, in hopes there to make head against the danger; but it is all in vain when evil pursues sinners with commission. They are told to send the alarm into the country, and to do what they can for their own safety: <hi type="italic">Blow the trumpet in Tekoa,</hi> a city which lay twelve miles north from Jerusalem. Let them be stirred up to stand upon their guard: <hi type="italic">Set up a sign of fire</hi> (that is, kindle the beacons) <hi type="italic">in Beth-haccerem,</hi> the <hi type="italic">house of the vineyard,</hi> which lay on a hill between Jerusalem and Tekoa. Prepare to make a vigorous resistance, <hi type="italic">for the evil appears out of the north.</hi> This may be taken ironically: "Betake yourselves to the best methods you can think of for your own preservation, but all shall be in vain; for, when you have done your best, it will be a great destruction, for it is in vain to contend with God's judgments." <div eID="gen17305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17306" type="x-p"/> 2. That the attempt upon them should be bold and formidable and such as they should be a very unequal match for. (1.) See what <hi type="italic">the daughter of Zion</hi> is, on whom the assault is made. She is compared <hi type="italic">to a comely and delicate woman</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.2">v. 2</reference>), bred up in every thing that is nice and soft, that will not set so much as the sole <hi type="italic">of her foot to the ground for tenderness and delicacy</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.56">Deut. xxviii. 56</reference>), nor suffer the wind to blow upon her; and, not being accustomed to hardship, she will be the less able either to resist the enemy (for those that make war must <hi type="italic">endure hardness</hi>) or to bear the destruction with that patience which is necessary to make it tolerable. The more we indulge ourselves in the pleasures of this life the more we disfit ourselves for the troubles of this life. (2.) See what the daughter of Babylon is, by whom the assault is made. The generals and their armies are compared to <hi type="italic">shepherds</hi> and <hi type="italic">their flocks</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.3">v. 3</reference>), in such numbers and in such order did they come, the soldiers following their leaders as the sheep their shepherds. The daughter of <hi type="italic">Zion dwelt at home</hi> (so some read it), expecting to be courted with love, but was invaded with fury. This comparing of the enemies to shepherds inclines me to embrace another reading, which some give of <reference osisRef="Jer.6.2">v. 2</reference>, <hi type="italic">The daughter of Zion is like a comely pasture-ground and a delicate land,</hi> which invite the shepherds to bring their flocks thither to graze; and as the shepherds easily make themselves masters of an open field, which (as was then usual in some parts) lies common, owned by none, <hi type="italic">pitch their tents</hi> in it, and their flocks quickly eat it bare, so shall the Chaldean army easily break in upon the land of Judah, force for themselves a free quarter where they please, and in a little time devour all. For the further illustration of this he shows, [1.] How God shall commission them to make this destruction even of the holy land and the holy city, which were his own possession. It is he that says (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.4">v. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">Prepare you war against her;</hi> for he is the <hi type="italic">Lord of hosts,</hi> that has all hosts at his command, and he has said (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.6">v. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">Hew you down trees, and cast a mount against Jerusalem,</hi> in order to the attacking of it. The Chaldeans have great power against Judah and Jerusalem, and yet they have no power but what is <hi type="italic">given them from above.</hi> God has marked out Jerusalem for destruction. He has said, "<hi type="italic">This is the city to be visited,</hi> visited in wrath, visited by the divine justice, and this is the time of her visitation." The day is coming when those that are careless and secure in sinful ways will certainly be visited. [2.] How they shall animate themselves and one another to execute that commission. God's counsels being against Jerusalem, which cannot be altered or disannulled, the councils of war which the enemies held are made to agree with his counsels. God having said, <hi type="italic">Prepare war against her,</hi> their determinations are made subservient to his; and, notwithstanding the distance of place and the many difficulties that lay in the way, it is soon resolved, <hi type="italic">nemine contradicente—unanimously. Arise, and let us go.</hi> Note, It is good to see how the counsel and decree of God are pursued and executed in the devices and designs of men, even theirs that know him not, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.6-Isa.10.7">Isa. x. 6, 7</reference>. In this campaign, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> They resolve to be very expeditious. They have no sooner resolved upon it than they address themselves to it; it shall never be said that they left any thing to be done towards it to-morrow which they could do to-day: <hi type="italic">Arise, let us go up at noon,</hi> though it be in the heat of the day; nay, (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.5">v. 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">Arise, let us go up at night,</hi> though it be in the dark. Nothing shall hinder them; they are resolved to <hi type="italic">lose no time.</hi> They are described as men in care to make despatch (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.4">v. 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Woe unto us, for the day goes away,</hi> and we are not going on with our work; <hi type="italic">the shadows of the evening are stretched out,</hi> and we sit still, and let slip the opportunity." O that we were thus eager in our spiritual work and warfare, thus afraid of losing time, or any opportunity, in taking the <hi type="italic">kingdom of heaven by violence!</hi> It is folly to trifle when we have an eternal salvation to work out, and the enemies of that salvation to fight against. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They confidently expect to be very successful: "<hi type="italic">Let us go up,</hi> and let us destroy her palaces and make ourselves masters of the wealth that is in them." It was not that they might fulfill God's counsels, but that they might fill their own treasures, that they were thus eager; yet God thereby served his own purposes. <div eID="gen17306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17307" type="x-p"/> II. The cause of this judgment assigned. It is all for their wickedness; they have brought it upon themselves; they must bear it, for they must bear the blame of it. They are thus oppressed because they have been oppressors; they have dealt hardly with one another, each in his turn, as they have had power and advantage, and now the enemy shall come and deal hardly with them all. This sin of oppression, and violence, and wrong-doing, is here charged upon them, 1. As a national sin (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> this city <hi type="italic">is to be visited,</hi> it is time to make inquisition, for <hi type="italic">she is wholly oppression in the midst of her.</hi> All orders and degrees of men, from the prince on the throne to the meanest master of a shop, were oppressive to those that were under them. Look which way you might, there were causes for complaints of this kind. 2. As a sin that had become in a manner natural to them (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.7">v. 7</reference>): She <hi type="italic">casts out wickedness,</hi> in all the instances of malice and mischievousness, <hi type="italic">as a fountain casts out her waters,</hi> so plentifully and constantly, the streams bitter and poisonous, like the fountain. The waters out of the fountain will not be restrained, but will find or force their way, nor will they be checked by laws or conscience in their violent proceedings. This is fitly applied to the corrupt heart of man in his natural state; it <hi type="italic">casts out wickedness,</hi> one evil imagination or other, as a fountain <hi type="italic">casts out her waters,</hi> naturally and easily; it is always flowing, and yet always full. 3. As that which had become a constant practice with them; <hi type="italic">Violence and spoil are heard in her.</hi> The cry of it had come up before God as that of Sodom: <hi type="italic">Before me continually are grief and wounds</hi>—the complaint of those that find themselves aggrieved, being unjustly wounded in their bodies or spirits, in their estates or reputation. Note, He that is the common Parent of mankind regards and resents, and sooner or later will revenge, the mischiefs and wrongs that men do to one another. <div eID="gen17307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17308" type="x-p"/> III. The counsel given them how to prevent this judgment. Fair warning is given now upon the whole matter: "<hi type="italic">Be thou instructed, O Jerusalem!</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.6.8">v. 8</reference>. Receive the instruction given thee both by the law of God and by the prophets; be wise at length for thyself." They knew very well what they had been instructed to do; nothing remained but to do it, for till then they could not be said to be instructed. The reason for this counsel is taken from the inevitable ruin they ran upon if they refused to comply with the instructions given them: <hi type="italic">Lest my soul depart,</hi> or <hi type="italic">be disjoined, from thee.</hi> This intimates what a tender affection and concern God had had for them; his very soul had been joined to them, and nothing but sin could disjoin it. Note, 1. The God of mercy is loth to depart even from a provoking people, and is earnest with them by true repentance and reformation to prevent things coming to that extremity. 2. Their case is very miserable from whom God's soul is disjoined; it intimates the loss not only of their outward blessings, but of those comforts and favours which are the more immediate and peculiar tokens of his love and presence. Compare this with that dreadful word (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.38">Heb. x. 38</reference>), <hi type="italic">If any man draw back, my soul shall have no pleasure in him.</hi> 3. Those whom God forsakes are certainly undone; when God's soul departs from Jerusalem she soon becomes desolate and uninhabited, <reference osisRef="Matt.23.38">Matt. xxiii. 38</reference>.
entries.3f252ed65ee9a532174b8f5acd5ef4da851e5af5: <div eID="gen17308" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Universal Corruption of the Age. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 608.)</title> <div sID="gen17309" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, They shall thoroughly glean the remnant of Israel as a vine: turn back thine hand as a grape-gatherer into the baskets. <hi type="super">10</hi> To whom shall I speak, and give warning, that they may hear? behold, their ear <hi type="italic">is</hi> uncircumcised, and they cannot hearken: behold, the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> is unto them a reproach; they have no delight in it. <hi type="super">11</hi> Therefore I am full of the fury of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; I am weary with holding in: I will pour it out upon the children abroad, and upon the assembly of young men together: for even the husband with the wife shall be taken, the aged with <hi type="italic">him that is</hi> full of days. <hi type="super">12</hi> And their houses shall be turned unto others, <hi type="italic">with their</hi> fields and wives together: for I will stretch out my hand upon the inhabitants of the land, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">13</hi> For from the least of them even unto the greatest of them every one <hi type="italic">is</hi> given to covetousness; and from the prophet even unto the priest every one dealeth falsely. <hi type="super">14</hi> They have healed also the hurt <hi type="italic">of the daughter</hi> of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no peace. <hi type="super">15</hi> Were they ashamed when they had committed abomination? nay, they were not at all ashamed, neither could they blush: therefore they shall fall among them that fall: at the time <hi type="italic">that</hi> I visit them they shall be cast down, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">16</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where <hi type="italic">is</hi> the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk <hi type="italic">therein.</hi> <hi type="super">17</hi> Also I set watchmen over you, <hi type="italic">saying,</hi> Hearken to the sound of the trumpet. But they said, We will not hearken. <div eID="gen17309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17310" type="x-p"/> The heads of this paragraph are the very same with those of the last; for precept must be upon precept and line upon line. <div eID="gen17310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17311" type="x-p"/> I. The ruin of Judah and Jerusalem is here threatened. We had before the haste which the Chaldea army made to the war (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.4-Jer.6.5">v. 4, 5</reference>); now here we have the havoc made by the war. How lamentable are the desolations here described! The enemy shall so long quarter among them, and be so insatiable in their thirst after blood and treasure, that they shall seize all they can meet with, and what escapes them at one time shall fall into their hands another (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall thoroughly glean the remnant of Israel as a vine;</hi> as the <hi type="italic">grape-gatherer,</hi> who is resolved to leave none behind, still <hi type="italic">turns back his hand into the baskets,</hi> to put more in, till he has gathered all, so that they be picked up by the enemy, though dispersed, though hid, and none of them shall escape their eye and hand. Perhaps the people, being <hi type="italic">given to covetousness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.13">v. 13</reference>), had not observed that law of God which forbade them to <hi type="italic">glean all their grapes</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.10">Lev. xix. 10</reference>), and now they themselves shall be in like manner <hi type="italic">thoroughly gleaned</hi> and shall either fall by the sword or go into captivity. This is explained <reference osisRef="Jer.6.11-Jer.6.12">v. 11, 12</reference>, where God's <hi type="italic">fury</hi> and his <hi type="italic">hand</hi> are said to be <hi type="italic">poured out</hi> and <hi type="italic">stretched out,</hi> in the fury and by the hand of the Chaldeans; for even wicked men are often made use of as God's hand (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.14">Ps. xvii. 14</reference>), and in their anger we may see God angry. Now see on whom the fury is poured out in full vials—<hi type="italic">upon the children abroad,</hi> or <hi type="italic">in the streets,</hi> where they are playing (<reference osisRef="Zech.8.5">Zech. viii. 5</reference>) or whither they run out innocently to look about them: the sword of the merciless Chaldeans shall not spare them, <reference osisRef="Jer.9.21">ch. ix. 21</reference>. The children perish in the calamity which the fathers' sins have procured. The execution shall likewise reach <hi type="italic">the assembly of young men,</hi> their merry meetings, their clubs which they keep up to strengthen one another's hands in wickedness; they shall be <hi type="italic">cut off together.</hi> Nor shall those only fall into the enemies' hands who meet for lewdness (<reference osisRef="Jer.5.7">ch. v. 7</reference>), but <hi type="italic">even the husband with the wife shall be taken,</hi> these two in bed together, and neither left, but both taken prisoners. And, as they have no compassion for the weak but fair sex, so they have none for the decrepit but venerable age: <hi type="italic">The old with the full of days,</hi> whose deaths can contribute no more to their safety than their lives to their service, who are not in a capacity to do them either good or harm, shall be either cut off or carried off. <hi type="italic">Their houses shall then be turned to others</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.12">v. 12</reference>); the conquerors shall dwell in their habitations, use their goods, and live upon their stores; their <hi type="italic">fields and vines</hi> shall fall <hi type="italic">together</hi> into their hands, as was threatened, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.30">Deut. xxviii. 30</reference>, &c. For God <hi type="italic">stretches out his hand upon the inhabitants of the land,</hi> and none can go out of the reach of it. Now as to this denunciation of God's wrath, 1. The prophet justifies himself in preaching thus terribly, for herein he dealt faithfully (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.11">v. 11</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I am full of the fury of the Lord,</hi> full of the thoughts and apprehensions of it, and am carried out with a powerful impulse, by the spirit of prophecy, to speak of it thus vehemently." He took no delight in threatening, nor was it any pleasure to him with such sermons as these to make those about him uneasy; but he could not contain himself; he was <hi type="italic">weary with holding in;</hi> he suppressed it as long as he could, as long as he durst, but he was so <hi type="italic">full of power by the Spirit of the Lord of hosts</hi> that he must speak, whether they will hear or whether they will forbear. Note, When ministers preach the terrors of the Lord according to the scripture we have no reason to be displeased at them; for they are but messengers, and must deliver their message, pleasing or unpleasing. 2. He condemns the false prophets who preached plausibly, for therein they flattered people and dealt unfaithfully (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.13-Jer.6.14">v. 13, 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">The priest and the prophet,</hi> who should be their watchmen and monitors, have <hi type="italic">dealt falsely,</hi> have not been true to their trust not told the people their faults and the danger they were in; they should have been their physicians, but they murdered their patients by letting them have their will, by giving them every thing that had a mind to, and flattering them into an opinion that they were in no danger (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.14">v. 14</reference>): They have <hi type="italic">healed the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly,</hi> or <hi type="italic">according to the cure of some slight hurt,</hi> skinning over the wound and never searching it to the bottom, applying lenitives only, when there was need of corrosives, soothing people in their sins, and giving them opiates to make them easy for the present, while the disease was preying upon the vitals. They said, "<hi type="italic">Peace peace</hi>—all shall be well." (if there were some thinking people among them, who were awake, and apprehensive of danger, they soon stopped their mouths with their priestly and prophetical authority, boldly averring that neither church nor state was in any danger), when <hi type="italic">there is no peace,</hi> because they went on in their idolatries and daring impieties. Note, Those are to be reckoned our false friends (that is, our worst and most dangerous enemies) who flatter us in a sinful way. <div eID="gen17311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17312" type="x-p"/> II. The sin of Judah and Jerusalem, which provoked God to bring this ruin upon them and justified him in it, is here declared. 1. They would by no means bear to be told of their faults, nor of the danger they were in. God bids the prophet give them warning of the judgment coming (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.9">v. 9</reference>), "but," says he, "<hi type="italic">to whom shall I speak and give warning?</hi> I cannot find out any that will so much as give me a patient hearing. I may give warning long enough, but these is nobody that will take warning. I cannot speak <hi type="italic">that they may hear,</hi> cannot speak to any purpose, or with any hope of success; for <hi type="italic">their ear is uncircumcised,</hi> it is carnal and fleshly, indisposed to receive the voice of God, so that <hi type="italic">they cannot hearken.</hi> They have, as it were, a thick skin grown over the organs of hearing, so that divine things might to as much purpose be spoken to a stone as to them. Nay, they are not only deaf to it, but prejudiced against it; therefore they cannot hear, because they are resolved that they will not: The <hi type="italic">word of the Lord is unto them a reproach;</hi> both the reproofs and the threatenings of the word are so;" they reckoned themselves wronged and affronted by both, and resented the prophet's plain-dealing with them as they would the most causeless slander and calumny. This was <hi type="italic">kicking against the pricks</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.9.5">Acts ix. 5</reference>), as the lawyers against the word of Christ, <reference osisRef="Luke.11.45">Luke xi. 45</reference>, <hi type="italic">Thus saying, thou repoachest us also.</hi> Note, Those reproofs that are counted reproaches, and hated as such, will certainly be turned into the heaviest woes. When it is here said, <hi type="italic">They have no delight in the word,</hi> more is implied than is expressed; "they have an antipathy to it; their hearts rise at it; it exasperates them, and enrages their corruptions, and they are ready to fly in the face and pull out the eyes of their reprovers." And how can those expect that the word of the Lord should speak any comfort to them who have no delight in it, but would rather be any where than within hearing of it? 2. They were inordinately set upon the world, and wholly carried away by the love of it (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.13">v. 13</reference>): "<hi type="italic">From the least of them even to the greatest,</hi> old and young, rich and poor, high and low, those of all ranks, professions, and employments, <hi type="italic">every one is given to covetousness,</hi> greedy of filthy lucre, all for what they can get, <hi type="italic">per fas per nefas—right or wrong;</hi>" and this made them oppressive and violent (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.6-Jer.6.7">v. 6, 7</reference>), for of those evils, as well as others, the love of money is the bitter root. Nay, and this hardened their hearts against the word of God and his prophets. It was the covetous Pharisees that derided Christ, <reference osisRef="Luke.16.14">Luke xvi. 14</reference>. 3. They had become impudent in sin and were past shame. After such a high charge of flagrant crimes proved upon them, it was very proper to ask (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.15">v. 15</reference>), <hi type="italic">Were they ashamed when they had committed</hi> all these <hi type="italic">abominations,</hi> which are such a reproach to their reason and religion? Did they blush at the conviction, and acknowledge that confusion of face belonged to them? If so, there is some hope of them yet. But, alas! there did not appear so much as this colour of virtue among them; their hearts were so hardened that <hi type="italic">they were not at all ashamed, neither could they blush,</hi> they had so brazened their faces. They even gloried in their wickedness, and openly confronted the convictions which should have humbled them and brought them to repentance. They resolved to face it out against God himself and not to own their guilt. Some refer this to the priests and prophets, who had healed the people slightly and told them that they should have peace, and yet were not ashamed of their treachery and falsehood, no, not when the event disproved them and gave them the lie. Those that are shameless are graceless and their case is hopeless. But those that will not submit to a penitential shame, nor take that to themselves as their due, shall not escape an utter ruin; for so it follows: <hi type="italic">Therefore they shall fall among</hi> those <hi type="italic">that fall;</hi> they shall have their portion with those that are quite undone; and, when God visits the nation in wrath, they shall be sure to be cast down and be made to tremble, because they would not blush. Note, Those that sin and cannot blush for it are in an evil case now, and it will be worse with them shortly. At first they hardened themselves and would not blush, afterwards they were so hardened that they could not. <hi type="italic">Quod unum habebant in malis bonum perdunt, peccandi verecundiam—they have lost the only good property which once blended itself with many bad ones, that is, shame for having done amiss.</hi>—Senec. De Vit. Beat. <div eID="gen17312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17313" type="x-p"/> III. They are put in mind of the good counsel which had been often given them, but in vain. They had a great deal said to them to little purpose, <div eID="gen17313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17314" type="x-p"/> 1. By way of advice concerning their duty, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.16">v. 16</reference>. God had been used to say to them, <hi type="italic">Stand in the ways and see.</hi> That is, (1.) He would have them to consider, not to proceed rashly, but to do as travellers in the road, who are in care to find the right way which will bring them to their journey's end, and therefore pause and enquire for it. If they have any reason to think that they have missed their way, they are not easy till they have obtained satisfaction. O that men would be thus <hi type="italic">wise for their souls,</hi> and would ponder the path of their feet, as those that believe lawful and unlawful are of no less consequence to us than the right way and the wrong are to a traveller! (2.) He would have them to consult antiquity, the observations and experiences of those that went before them: "<hi type="italic">Ask for the old paths, enquire of the former age</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.8.8">Job viii. 8</reference>), <hi type="italic">ask thy father, thy elders</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.7">Deut. xxxii. 7</reference>), and thou wilt find that the way of godliness and righteousness has always been the way which God has owned and blessed and in which men have prospered. Ask for the <hi type="italic">old paths,</hi> the paths prescribed by the law of God, the written word, that true standard of antiquity. Ask for the paths that the patriarchs travelled in before you, Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob; and, as you hope to inherit the promises made to them, tread in their steps. <hi type="italic">Ask for the old paths, Where is the good way?</hi>" We must not be guided merely by antiquity, as if the plea of prescription and long usage were alone sufficient to justify our path. No; there is an <hi type="italic">old way which wicked men have trodden,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.22.15">Job xxii. 15</reference>. But, when we ask for the old paths, it is only in order to find out the <hi type="italic">good way,</hi> the highway of the upright. Note, The way of religion and godliness is a good old way, the way that all the saints in all ages have walked in. (3.) He would have them to resolve to act according to the result of these enquiries: "When you have found out which is the good way, <hi type="italic">walk therein,</hi> practise accordingly, keep closely to that way, proceed, and persevere in it." Some make this counsel to be given them with reference to the struggles that were between the true and false prophets, between those that said they should have peace and those that told them trouble was at the door; they pretended they knew not which to believe: "<hi type="italic">Stand in the way,</hi>" says God, "and see, and enquire, which of these two agrees with the written word and the usual methods of God's providence, which of these directs you to the good way, and do accordingly." (4.) He assures them that, if they do thus, it will secure the welfare and satisfaction of their own souls: "<hi type="italic">Walk in the good old way</hi> and you will find your walking in that way will be easy and pleasant; you will enjoy both your God and yourselves, and the way will lead you to true rest. Though it cost you some pains to walk in that way, you will find an abundant recompence at your journey's end." (5.) He laments that this good counsel, which was so rational in itself and so proper for them, could not find acceptance: "<hi type="italic">But they said, We will not walk therein,</hi> not only we will not be at the pains to enquire <hi type="italic">which is the good way,</hi> the <hi type="italic">good old way;</hi> but when it is told us, and we have nothing to say to the contrary but that it is the right way, yet we will not deny ourselves and our humours so far as to <hi type="italic">walk in it.</hi>" Thus multitudes are ruined for ever by downright wilfulness. <div eID="gen17314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17315" type="x-p"/> 2. By way of admonition concerning their danger. Because they would not be ruled by fair reasoning, God takes another method with them; by less judgments he threatens greater, and sends his prophets to give them this explication of them, and to frighten them with an apprehension of the danger they were in (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.17">v. 17</reference>); <hi type="italic">Also I set watchmen over you.</hi> God's ministers are watchmen, and it is a great mercy to have them set over us in the Lord. Now observe here, (1.) The fair warning given by these watchmen. This was the burden of their song; they cried again and again, <hi type="italic">Hearken to the sound of the trumpet.</hi> God, in his providence, sounds the trumpet (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.14">Zech. ix. 14</reference>); the watchmen hear it themselves and are affected with it (<reference osisRef="Jer.4.19">Jer. iv. 19</reference>), and they are to call upon others to hearken to it too, to hear the Lord's controversy, to observe the voice of Providence, to improve it, and answer the intentions of it. (2.) This fair warning slighted: "<hi type="italic">But they said, We will not hearken;</hi> we will not hear, we will not heed, we will not believe; the prophets may as well save themselves and us the trouble." The reason why sinners perish is because they <hi type="italic">do not hearken to the sound of the trumpet;</hi> and the reason why they do not is because they will not; and they have no reason to give why they will not but because they will not, that is, they are herein most unreasonable. One may more easily deal with ten men's reasons than one man's will.
entries.6d1861bc2db70b9639ee6e7443250e2050389531: <div eID="gen17315" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Equity of Divine Judgments; Punishment Predicted. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 608.)</title> <div sID="gen17316" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> Therefore hear, ye nations, and know, O congregation, what <hi type="italic">is</hi> among them. <hi type="super">19</hi> Hear, O earth: behold, I will bring evil upon this people, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the fruit of their thoughts, because they have not hearkened unto my words, nor to my law, but rejected it. <hi type="super">20</hi> To what purpose cometh there to me incense from Sheba, and the sweet cane from a far country? your burnt offerings <hi type="italic">are</hi> not acceptable, nor your sacrifices sweet unto me. <hi type="super">21</hi> Therefore thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , Behold, I will lay stumbling-blocks before this people, and the fathers and the sons together shall fall upon them; the neighbour and his friend shall perish. <hi type="super">22</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , Behold, a people cometh from the north country, and a great nation shall be raised from the sides of the earth. <hi type="super">23</hi> They shall lay hold on bow and spear; they <hi type="italic">are</hi> cruel, and have no mercy; their voice roareth like the sea; and they ride upon horses, set in array as men for war against thee, O daughter of Zion. <hi type="super">24</hi> We have heard the fame thereof: our hands wax feeble: anguish hath taken hold of us, <hi type="italic">and</hi> pain, as of a woman in travail. <hi type="super">25</hi> Go not forth into the field, nor walk by the way; for the sword of the enemy <hi type="italic">and</hi> fear <hi type="italic">is</hi> on every side. <hi type="super">26</hi> O daughter of my people, gird <hi type="italic">thee</hi> with sackcloth, and wallow thyself in ashes: make thee mourning, <hi type="italic">as for</hi> an only son, most bitter lamentation: for the spoiler shall suddenly come upon us. <hi type="super">27</hi> I have set thee <hi type="italic">for</hi> a tower <hi type="italic">and</hi> a fortress among my people, that thou mayest know and try their way. <hi type="super">28</hi> They <hi type="italic">are</hi> all grievous revolters, walking with slanders: <hi type="italic">they are</hi> brass and iron; they <hi type="italic">are</hi> all corrupters. <hi type="super">29</hi> The bellows are burned, the lead is consumed of the fire; the founder melteth in vain: for the wicked are not plucked away. <hi type="super">30</hi> Reprobate silver shall <hi type="italic">men</hi> call them, because the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath rejected them. <div eID="gen17316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17317" type="x-p"/> Here, I. God appeals to all the neighbours, nay, to the whole world, concerning the equity of his proceedings against Judah and Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.18-Jer.6.19">v. 18, 19</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Hear, you nations, and know</hi> particularly, <hi type="italic">O congregation</hi> of the mighty, the great men of the nations, that take cognizance of the affairs of states about you and make remarks upon them. Observe now what is doing among those of Judah and Jerusalem; you hear of the desolations brought upon them, the earth rings of it, trembles under it; you all wonder that <hi type="italic">I</hi> should <hi type="italic">bring evil upon this people,</hi> that are in covenant with me, that profess relation to me, that have worshipped me, and been highly favoured by me; you are ready to ask, <hi type="italic">Wherefore has the Lord done thus to this land?</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.29.24">Deut. xxix. 24</reference>. Know then," 1. "That it is the natural product of their devices. The evil brought upon them is <hi type="italic">the fruit of their thought.</hi> They thought to strengthen themselves by their alliance with foreigners, and by that very thing they weakened and diminished themselves, they betrayed and exposed themselves." 2. "That it is the just punishment of their disobedience and rebellion. God does but execute upon them the curse of the law for their violation of its commands. It is because <hi type="italic">they have not hearkened to my words nor to my law,</hi> nor regarded a word I have said to them, but rejected it all. They would never have been ruined thus by the judgments of God's hand if they had not refused to be ruled by the judgments of his mouth: therefore you cannot say that they have any wrong done them." <div eID="gen17317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17318" type="x-p"/> II. God rejects their plea, by which they insisted upon their external services as sufficient to atone for all their sins. Alas! it is a frivolous plea (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.20">v. 20</reference>): "<hi type="italic">To what purpose come there to me incense and sweet cane,</hi> to be burnt for a perfume on the golden altar, though it was the best of the kind, and far-fetched? What care I for <hi type="italic">your burnt-offerings</hi> and <hi type="italic">your sacrifices?</hi>" They not only cannot profit God (no sacrifice does, <reference osisRef="Ps.50.9">Ps. l. 9</reference>), but they do not please him, for none does this but the sacrifice of the upright; that of the wicked is an <hi type="italic">abomination to him.</hi> Sacrifice and incense were appointed to excite their repentance, and to direct them to a Mediator, and assist their faith in him. Where this good use was made of them they were acceptable, God had respect to them and to those that offered them. But when they were offered with an opinion that thereby they made God their debtor, and purchased a license to go on in sin, they were so far from being pleasing to God that they were a provocation to him. <div eID="gen17318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17319" type="x-p"/> III. He foretels the desolation that was now coming upon them. 1. God designs their ruin because they hate to be reformed (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will lay stumbling-blocks before this people,</hi> occasions of falling not into sin, but into trouble. Those whom God has marked for destruction he perplexes and embarrasses in their counsels, and obstructs and retards all the methods they take for their own safety. The parties of the enemy, which they met with wherever they went, were stumbling-blocks to them; in ever corner they stumbled upon them and were dashed to pieces by them: <hi type="italic">The fathers and the sons together shall fall upon them;</hi> neither the fathers with their wisdom, nor the sons with their strength and courage, shall escape them, or get over them. The sons that sinned with their fathers fall with them. Even the <hi type="italic">neighbour and his friend shall perish</hi> and not be able to help either themselves or one another. 2. He will make use of the Chaldeans as instruments of it; for whatever work God has to do he will find out proper instruments for the doing of it. This is a people fetched <hi type="italic">from the north, from the sides of the earth.</hi> Babylon itself lay a great way off northward; and some of the countries that were subject to the king of Babylon, out of which his army was levied, lay much further. These must be employed in this service, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.22-Jer.6.23">v. 22, 23</reference>. For, (1.) It is a people very numerous, <hi type="italic">a great nation,</hi> which will make their invasion the more formidable. (2.) It is a warlike people. <hi type="italic">They lay hold on bow and spear,</hi> and at this time know how to use them, for they are used to them. <hi type="italic">They ride upon horses,</hi> and therefore they march the more swiftly, and in battle press the harder. No nation had yet brought into the field a better cavalry that the Chaldeans. (3.) It is a barbarous people. They <hi type="italic">are cruel and have no mercy,</hi> being greedy of prey and flushed with victory. They take a pride in frightening all about them; their voice <hi type="italic">roars like the sea.</hi> And, (4.) They have a particular design upon Judah and Jerusalem, in hopes greatly to enrich themselves with the spoil of that famous country. They are <hi type="italic">set in array against thee, O daughter of Zion!</hi> The sins of God's professing people make them an easy prey to those that are God's enemies as well as theirs. <div eID="gen17319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17320" type="x-p"/> IV. He describes the very great consternation which Judah and Jerusalem should be in upon the approach of this formidable enemy, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.24-Jer.6.26">v. 24-26</reference>. 1. They own themselves in a fright, upon the first intelligence brought them of the approach of the enemy: "When <hi type="italic">we have but heard the fame thereof our hands wax feeble,</hi> and we have no heart to make any resistance; <hi type="italic">anguish has taken hold of us,</hi> and we are immediately in an extremity of pain, like that of <hi type="italic">a woman in travail.</hi>" Note, Sense of guilt quite dispirits men, upon the approach of any threatening trouble. What can those hope to do for themselves who have made God their enemy? 2. They confine themselves by consent to their houses, not daring to show their heads abroad; for, though they could not but expect that the sword of the enemy would at last find them out there, yet they would rather die tamely and meanly there than run any venture, either by fight or flight, to help themselves. Thus they say one to another, "<hi type="italic">Go not forth into the field,</hi> no not to fetch in your provision thence, <hi type="italic">nor walk by the way;</hi> dare not to go to church or market, it is at your peril if you do, for the <hi type="italic">sword of the enemy,</hi> and the fear of it, are <hi type="italic">on every side;</hi> the <hi type="italic">highways are unoccupied,</hi> as in Jael's time," <reference osisRef="Judg.5.6">Judg. v. 6</reference>. Let this remind us, when we travel the roads in safety and there is none to make us afraid, to bless God for our share in the public tranquillity. 3. The prophet calls upon them sadly to lament the desolations that were coming upon them. He was himself the lamenting prophet, and called upon his people to join with him in his lamentations: "<hi type="italic">O daughter of my people,</hi> hear thy God calling thee to weeping and mourning, and answer his call: do not only put on sackcloth for a day, but gird it on for thy constant wear; do not only put ashes on thy head, but <hi type="italic">wallow thyself in ashes;</hi> put thyself into close mourning, and use all the tokens of bitter lamentation, not forced and for show only, but with the greatest sincerity, as parents <hi type="italic">mourn for an only son,</hi> and think themselves comfortless because they are childless. Thus do thou lament for <hi type="italic">the spoiler that suddenly comes upon us.</hi> Though he has not come yet, he is <hi type="italic">coming,</hi> the decree has <hi type="italic">gone forth:</hi> let us therefore meet the execution of it with a suitable sadness." As saints may rejoice in hope of God's mercies, though they see them only in the promise, so sinners must mourn for fear of God's judgments, though they see them only in the threatenings. <div eID="gen17320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17321" type="x-p"/> V. He constitutes the prophet a judge over this people that now stand upon their trial: as <reference osisRef="Jer.1.10">ch. i. 10</reference>, <hi type="italic">I have set thee over the nations;</hi> so here, <hi type="italic">I have set thee for a tower,</hi> or as a sentinel, or a watchman, upon a tower, <hi type="italic">among my people,</hi> as an inspector of their actions, <hi type="italic">that thou mayest know, and try their way,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.6.27">v. 27</reference>. Not that God needed any to inform him concerning them; on the contrary, the prophet knew little of them in comparison but by the spirit of prophecy. But thus God appeals to the prophet himself, and his own observation concerning their character, that he might be fully satisfied in the equity of God's proceedings against them and with the more assurance give them warning of the judgments coming. God set him for a tower, conspicuous to all and attacked by many, but made him a <hi type="italic">fortress,</hi> a <hi type="italic">strong tower,</hi> gave him courage to stem the tide and bear the shock of their displeasure. Those that will be faithful reprovers have need to be firm as fortresses. Now in trying their way he will find two things:—1. That they are wretchedly debauched (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.28">v. 28</reference>): <hi type="italic">They are all grievous revolters, revolters of revolters</hi> (so the word is), the worst of revolters, as a <hi type="italic">servant of servants</hi> is the meanest servant. They have a revolting heart, have deeply revolted, and revolt more and more. They seemed to start fair, but they revolt and start back. They <hi type="italic">walk with slanders;</hi> they make nothing of belying and backbiting one another, nay, they make a perfect trade of it; it is their constant course, and they govern themselves by the slanders they hear, hating those that they hear ill-spoken of, though ever so unjustly. They are <hi type="italic">brass and iron,</hi> base metals, and there is nothing in them that is valuable. They were as silver and gold, but they have degenerated. Nay, as <hi type="italic">they are all revolters,</hi> so <hi type="italic">they are all corrupters,</hi> not only debauched themselves, but industrious to debauch others, to corrupt them as they themselves are corrupt; nay, to make them seven times more the children of hell than themselves. It is often so; sinners soon become tempters. 2. That they would never be reclaimed and reformed; it was in vain to think of reforming them, for various methods had been tried with them, and all to no purpose, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.29-Jer.6.30">v. 29, 30</reference>. He compares them to ore that was supposed to have some good metal in it, and was therefore put into the furnace by the refiner, who used all his art, and took abundance of pains, about it, but it proved all dross, nothing of any value could be extracted out of it. God by his prophets and by his providences had used the most proper means to refine this people and to purify them from their wickedness; but it was all in vain. By the continual preaching of the word, and in a series of afflictions, they had been kept in a constant fire, but all to no purpose. <hi type="italic">The bellows</hi> have been still kept so near the fire, to blow it, that they <hi type="italic">are burnt</hi> with the heat of it, or they are quite worn out with long use and thrown into the fire as good for nothing. The prophets have preached their throats sore with crying aloud against the sins of Israel, and yet they are not convinced and humbled. The <hi type="italic">lead,</hi> which was then used in refining silver, as quicksilver is now, <hi type="italic">is consumed of the fire,</hi> and has not done its work. <hi type="italic">The founder melts in vain;</hi> his labour is lost, <hi type="italic">for the wicked are not plucked away,</hi> no care is taken to separate between the precious and the vile, to purge out the old leaven, to cast out of communion those who, being corrupt themselves, are in danger of infecting others. Or, <hi type="italic">Their wickednesses are not removed</hi> (so some read it); they are still as bad as ever, and nothing will prevail to part between them and their sins. They will not be brought off from their idolatries and immoralities by all they have heard, and all they have felt, of the wrath of God against them; and therefore that doom is passed upon them (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.30">v. 30</reference>): <hi type="italic">Reprobate silver shall they be called,</hi> useless and worthless; they glitter as if they had some silver in them, but there is nothing of real virtue or goodness to be found among them; and for this reason <hi type="italic">the Lord has rejected them.</hi> He will no more own them as his people, nor look for any good from them; he will <hi type="italic">take them away like dross</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.119">Ps. cxix. 119</reference>), and prepare a consuming fire for those that would not be purified by a refining fire. By this it appears, (1.) That God has <hi type="italic">no pleasure in the death</hi> and ruin of sinners, for he tries all ways and methods with them to prevent their destruction and qualify them for salvation. Both his ordinances and his providences have a tendency this way, to part between them and their sins; and yet with many it is all lost labour. <hi type="italic">We have piped unto you, and you have not danced; we have mourned unto you, and you have not wept.</hi> Therefore, (2.) God will be justified in the death of sinners and all the blame will lie upon themselves. He did not reject them till he had used all proper means to reform them; did not cast them off so long as there was any hope of them, nor abandon them as dross till it appeared that they were <hi type="italic">reprobate silver.</hi>  <chapter eID="Jer.6"/> <div eID="gen17321" type="x-p"/>

entries.600cfe66ed6b73a4189333c3aa7877949f6c32e1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9712"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 6</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jer.6.1-Jer.6.30">Jr 6:1-30</reference>. Zion's Foes Prepare War against Her: Her Sins Are the Cause.</title> <div sID="gen17146" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9712"/><hi type="bold">1. Benjamin--</hi>Jerusalem was situated in the tribe of Benjamin, which was here separated from that of Judah by the valley of Hinnom. Though it was inhabited partly by Benjamites, partly by men of Judah, he addresses the former as being his own countrymen.<div eID="gen17146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17147" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blow ... trumpet ... Tekoa--</hi>Tikehu, Tekoa form a play on sounds. The birthplace of Amos.<div eID="gen17147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17148" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Beth-haccerem--</hi>meaning in Hebrew, "vineyard-house." It and Tekoa were a few miles south of Jerusalem. As the enemy came from the north, the inhabitants of the surrounding country would naturally flee southwards. The fire-signal on the hills gave warning of danger approaching. <div eID="gen17148" type="x-p"/>
entries.5a83cf31e5ef3d1ed59dbce567cf5c5b83cd97b8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9713"/><div sID="gen17149" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9713"/><hi type="bold">2. likened--</hi>rather, "I lay waste." Literally, "O comely and delicate one, I lay waste the daughter of Zion," that is, "thee." So <reference osisRef="Zech.3.9">Zec 3:9</reference>, "before Joshua," that is, "before thee" [Maurer]. <div eID="gen17149" type="x-p"/>
entries.91db61280152feb1282f4efcbc27a658b86c64dc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9714"/><div sID="gen17150" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9714"/><hi type="bold">3. shepherds--</hi>hostile leaders with their armies (<reference osisRef="Jer.1.15">Jr 1:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.17">4:17</reference>; 49:20; 50:45).<div eID="gen17150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17151" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">feed--</hi>They shall consume each one all that is near him; literally, "his hand," that is, the place which he occupies (<reference osisRef="Num.2.17">Nu 2:17</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="Isa.56.5">Is 56:5</reference>). <div eID="gen17151" type="x-p"/>
entries.7d824ab6438786704692038f46739f111c76ea97: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9715"/><div sID="gen17152" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9715"/>4-5. The invading soldiers encourage one another to the attack on Jerusalem.<div eID="gen17152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17153" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Prepare--</hi>literally, "Sanctify" war, that is, Proclaim it formally with solemn rites; the invasion was solemnly ordered by God (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.13.3">Is 13:3</reference>).<div eID="gen17153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17154" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">at noon--</hi>the hottest part of the day when attacks were rarely made (<reference osisRef="Jer.15.8">Jr 15:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.20.16">20:16</reference>). Even at this time they wished to attack, such is their eagerness.<div eID="gen17154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17155" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Woe unto us--</hi>The words of the invaders, mourning the approach of night which would suspend their hostile operations; still, even in spite of the darkness, at night they renew the attack (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.5">Jr 6:5</reference>). <div eID="gen17155" type="x-p"/>
entries.5f0323f247c3676e18b739978664d577a53b4d2e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9716"/><div sID="gen17156" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9716"/><hi type="bold">6. cast--</hi>Hebrew, "pour out"; referring to the emptying of the baskets of earth to make the mound, formed of "trees" and earthwork, to overtop the city walls. The "trees" were also used to make warlike engines.<div eID="gen17156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17157" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">this--</hi>pointing the invaders to Jerusalem.<div eID="gen17157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17158" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">visited--</hi>that is, punished.<div eID="gen17158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17159" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wholly oppression--</hi>or join "wholly" with "visited," that is, she is altogether (in her whole extent) to be punished [Maurer]. <div eID="gen17159" type="x-p"/>
entries.3c85ab012222b386d8a186e8f28f190e1bebf936: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9717"/><div sID="gen17160" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9717"/><hi type="bold">7. fountain--</hi>rather, a well dug, from which water springs; distinct from a natural spring or fountain.<div eID="gen17160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17161" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">casteth out--</hi>causeth to flow; literally, "causeth to dig," the cause being put for the effect (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.16">2Ki 21:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.24">24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.57.20">Is 57:20</reference>).<div eID="gen17161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17162" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">me--</hi>Jehovah. <div eID="gen17162" type="x-p"/>
entries.9a0f2bbea47507cfd758d7691293e06f88a1785f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9718"/><div sID="gen17163" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9718"/>8. Tender appeal in the midst of threats.<div eID="gen17163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17164" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">depart--</hi>Hebrew, "be torn away"; Jehovah's affection making Him unwilling to depart; His attachment to Jerusalem was such that an effort was needed to tear Himself from it (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.18">Eze 23:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.9.12">Ho 9:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.11.8">11:8</reference>). <div eID="gen17164" type="x-p"/>
entries.eb8998d265bd30ca4e1cf967ede5f20dc5d8e102: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9719"/><div sID="gen17165" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9719"/>9. The Jews are the grapes, their enemies the unsparing gleaners.<div eID="gen17165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17166" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">turn back ... hand--</hi>again and again bring freshly gathered handfuls to the baskets; referring to the repeated carrying away of captives to Babylon (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.28-Jer.52.30">Jr 52:28-30</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.14">2Ki 24:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.11">25:11</reference>). <div eID="gen17166" type="x-p"/>
entries.fdc8a0706de322b202765b0ee9da00c2a5ab3c14: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9720"/><div sID="gen17167" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9720"/><hi type="bold">10. ear is uncircumcised--</hi>closed against the precepts of God by the foreskin of carnality (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.41">Le 26:41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.7">Eze 44:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.7.51">Ac 7:51</reference>).<div eID="gen17167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17168" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">word ... reproach--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.20.8">Jr 20:8</reference>). <div eID="gen17168" type="x-p"/>
entries.5c341e76833ca2253384915162deef149b4b6df7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9721"/><div sID="gen17169" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9721"/><hi type="bold">11. fury of ... Lord--</hi>His denunciations against Judah communicated to the prophet.<div eID="gen17169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17170" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">weary with holding in--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.20.9">Jr 20:9</reference>).<div eID="gen17170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17171" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I will pour--</hi>or else imperative: the command of God (see <reference osisRef="Jer.6.12">Jr 6:12</reference>), "Pour it out" [Maurer].<div eID="gen17171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17172" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">aged ... full of days--</hi>The former means one becoming old; the latter a decrepit old man [Maurer] (<reference osisRef="Job.5.26">Job 5:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.65.20">Is 65:20</reference>). <div eID="gen17172" type="x-p"/>
entries.529aa9dc912d82b48a5cf9018a3b79c86ee0d081: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9722"/><div sID="gen17173" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9722"/>12. The very punishments threatened by Moses in the event of disobedience to God (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.30">De 28:30</reference>).<div eID="gen17173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17174" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">turned--</hi>transferred. <div eID="gen17174" type="x-p"/>
entries.df936801583a37dca7af92886357e51dd93cb69e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9723"/><div sID="gen17175" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9723"/>13. (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.10">Jr 8:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.56.11">Is 56:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.3.11">Mi 3:11</reference>). <div eID="gen17175" type="x-p"/>
entries.b609d6b624025a7e030f831a201c7adcdb8dbdcf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9724"/><div sID="gen17176" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9724"/><hi type="bold">14. hurt--</hi>the spiritual wound.<div eID="gen17176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17177" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">slightly--</hi>as if it were but a slight wound; or, in a slight manner, pronouncing all sound where there is no soundness.<div eID="gen17177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17178" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">saying--</hi>namely, the prophets and priests (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.13">Jr 6:13</reference>). Whereas they ought to warn the people of impending judgments and the need of repentance, they say there is nothing to fear.<div eID="gen17178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17179" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">peace--</hi>including soundness. All is sound in the nation's moral state, so all will be peace as to its political state (<reference osisRef="Jer.4.10">Jr 4:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.8.11">8:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.14.13">14:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.17">23:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.13.5">Eze 13:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.13.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.28">22:28</reference>). <div eID="gen17179" type="x-p"/>
entries.b11df3eb27eea0a86c81ceffee9dd7aa8bcc4106: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9725"/><div sID="gen17180" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9725"/>15. Rosenmuller translates, "They ought to have been ashamed, because ... but," &c.; the Hebrew verb often expressing, not the action, but the duty to perform it (<reference osisRef="Gen.20.9">Ge 20:9</reference>; Mal 2:7). Maurer translates, "They shall be put to shame, for they commit abomination; nay (the prophet correcting himself), there is no shame in them" (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.3">Jr 3:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.8.12">8:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.7">Eze 3:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.5">Zep 3:5</reference>).<div eID="gen17180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17181" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">them that fall--</hi>They shall fall with the rest of their people who are doomed to fall, that is, I will now cease from words; I will execute vengeance [Calvin]. <div eID="gen17181" type="x-p"/>
entries.41b4db22fce7cbbc4dc13c42ac5be8379496f38f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9726"/><div sID="gen17182" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9726"/>16. Image from travellers who have lost their road, stopping and inquiring which is the right way on which they once had been, but from which they have wandered.<div eID="gen17182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17183" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">old paths--</hi>Idolatry and apostasy are the modern way; the worship of God the old way. Evil is not coeval with good, but a modern degeneracy from good. The forsaking of God is not, in a true sense, a "way cast up" at all (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.15">Jr 18:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.139.24">Psa 139:24</reference>; Mal 4:4).<div eID="gen17183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17184" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rest--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.28.12">Is 28:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.11.29">Mt 11:29</reference>). <div eID="gen17184" type="x-p"/>
entries.509216066e393bd3aa902f94f3ecc01fc60db048: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9727"/><div sID="gen17185" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9727"/><hi type="bold">17. watchmen--</hi>prophets, whose duty it was to announce impending calamities, so as to lead the people to repentance (<reference osisRef="Isa.21.11">Is 21:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.58.1">58:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.17">Eze 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.1">Ha 2:1</reference>). <div eID="gen17185" type="x-p"/>
entries.630864a4e8bb258ef5987b7d57e978d5583a242f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9728"/><div sID="gen17186" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9728"/><hi type="bold">18. congregation--</hi>parallel to "nations"; it therefore means the gathered peoples who are invited to be witnesses as to how great is the perversity of the Israelites (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.16">Jr 6:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.17">17</reference>), and that they deserve the severe punishment about to be inflicted on them (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.19">Jr 6:19</reference>).<div eID="gen17186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17187" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">what is among them--</hi>what deeds are committed by the Israelites (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.16">Jr 6:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.17">17</reference>) [Maurer]. Or, "what punishments are about to be inflicted on them" [Calvin]. <div eID="gen17187" type="x-p"/>
entries.7e09604fbc51b80113aa5f2fd86066378a9c42be: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9729"/><div sID="gen17188" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9729"/>19. (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.2">Is 1:2</reference>).<div eID="gen17188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17189" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fruit of ... thoughts--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.1.31">Pr 1:31</reference>).<div eID="gen17189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17190" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nor to my law, but rejected it--</hi>literally, "and (as to) My law they have rejected it." The same construction occurs in <reference osisRef="Gen.22.24">Ge 22:24</reference>. <div eID="gen17190" type="x-p"/>
entries.ed9b0fe47e7fc32e9f300bb4718896cc59ba4be2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9730"/><div sID="gen17191" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9730"/>20. Literally, "To what purpose is this to Me, that incense cometh to Me?"<div eID="gen17191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17192" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">incense ... cane--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.43.24">Is 43:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.60.6">60:6</reference>). No external services are accepted by God without obedience of the heart and life (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.21">Jr 7:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.50.7-Ps.50.9">Psa 50:7-9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.11">Is 1:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.6.6">Mi 6:6</reference>, &c.).<div eID="gen17192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17193" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sweet ... sweet--</hi>antithesis. Your sweet cane is not sweet to Me. The calamus. <div eID="gen17193" type="x-p"/>
entries.475f90fe0d9a75a15de76832000beb724195fe97: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9731"/><div sID="gen17194" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9731"/><hi type="bold">21. stumbling-blocks--</hi>instruments of the Jews' ruin (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.21.44">Mt 21:44</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.8.14">Is 8:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.8">1Pe 2:8</reference>). God Himself ("I") lays them before the reprobate (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.22">Psa 69:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.1.28">Ro 1:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.9">11:9</reference>).<div eID="gen17194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17195" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fathers ... sons ... neighbour ... friend--</hi>indiscriminate ruin. <div eID="gen17195" type="x-p"/>
entries.805eaa272cd982ec5ab7c911fed425d7e9c4deb8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9732"/><div sID="gen17196" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9732"/><hi type="bold">22. north ... sides of the earth--</hi>The ancients were little acquainted with the north; therefore it is called the remotest regions (as the Hebrew for "sides" ought to be translated, see on <reference osisRef="Isa.14.13">Is 14:13</reference>) of the earth. The Chaldees are meant (<reference osisRef="Jer.1.15">Jr 1:15</reference>; 5:15). It is striking that the very same calamities which the Chaldeans had inflicted on Zion are threatened as the retribution to be dealt in turn to themselves by Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.41-Jer.50.43">Jr 50:41-43</reference>). <div eID="gen17196" type="x-p"/>
entries.04180c85ed0e900db4d54e40d2a3b79fc0857303: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9733"/><div sID="gen17197" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9733"/><hi type="bold">23. like the sea--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.5.30">Is 5:30</reference>).<div eID="gen17197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17198" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as men for war--</hi>not that they were like warriors, for they were warriors; but "arrayed most perfectly as warriors" [Maurer]. <div eID="gen17198" type="x-p"/>
entries.882989f6aecafe65b61e12e003d3cacfe6f6e701: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9734"/><div sID="gen17199" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9734"/><hi type="bold">24. fame thereof--</hi>the report of them. <div eID="gen17199" type="x-p"/>
entries.3c6f76df227dab0f1860a0fc4d8fb8b225b2dfbc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9735"/><div sID="gen17200" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9735"/>25. He addresses "the daughter of Zion" (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.23">Jr 6:23</reference>); caution to the citizens of Jerusalem not to expose themselves to the enemy by going outside of the city walls.<div eID="gen17200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17201" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sword of the enemy--</hi>literally, "there is a sword to the enemy"; the enemy hath a sword. <div eID="gen17201" type="x-p"/>
entries.1cff4b3b7f2a20be7aae4efc0d95d0a6fb4b68de: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9736"/><div sID="gen17202" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9736"/><hi type="bold">26. wallow ... in ashes--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.25.34">Jr 25:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.1.10">Mi 1:10</reference>). As they usually in mourning only "cast ashes on the head," wallowing in them means something more, namely, so entirely to cover one's self with ashes as to be like one who had rolled in them (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.30">Eze 27:30</reference>).<div eID="gen17202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17203" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as for an only son--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Amos.8.10">Am 8:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.12.10">Zec 12:10</reference>).<div eID="gen17203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17204" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lamentation--</hi>literally, "lamentation expressed by beating the breast." <div eID="gen17204" type="x-p"/>
entries.9c2e526534b10ead6a5e29c65e6e2bbb0ab68f9f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9737"/><div sID="gen17205" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9737"/><hi type="bold">27. tower ... fortress--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.1.18">Jr 1:18</reference>), rather, "an assayer (and) explorer." By a metaphor from metallurgy in <reference osisRef="Jer.6.27-Jer.6.30">Jr 6:27-30</reference>, Jehovah, in conclusion, confirms the prophet in his office, and the latter sums up the description of the reprobate people on whom he had to work. The Hebrew for "assayer" (English Version, "tower") is from a root "to try" metals. "Explorer" (English Version, "fortress") is from an Arabic root, "keen-sighted"; or a Hebrew root, "cutting," that is, separating the metal from the dross [Ewald]. Gesenius translates as English Version, "fortress," which does not accord with the previous "assayer." <div eID="gen17205" type="x-p"/>
entries.b2be4b84158f90506b90f581477be58ee044b474: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9738"/><div sID="gen17206" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9738"/><hi type="bold">28. grievous revolters--</hi>literally, "contumacious of the contumacious," that is, most contumacious, the Hebrew mode of expressing a superlative. So "the strong among the mighty," that is, the strongest (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.21">Eze 32:21</reference>). See <reference osisRef="Jer.5.23">Jr 5:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.4.16">Ho 4:16</reference>.<div eID="gen17206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17207" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">walking with slanders--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.9.4">Jr 9:4</reference>). "Going about for the purpose of slandering" [Maurer].<div eID="gen17207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17208" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brass, &c.--</hi>that is, copper. It and "iron" being the baser and harder metals express the debased and obdurate character of the Jews (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.4">Is 48:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.60.17">60:17</reference>). <div eID="gen17208" type="x-p"/>
entries.488f72c329c61941c8c46f773a7e6a6314c2c2a9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9739"/><div sID="gen17209" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9739"/><hi type="bold">29. bellows ... burned--</hi>So intense a heat is made that the very bellows are almost set on fire. Rosenmuller translates not so well from a Hebrew root, "pant" or "snort," referring to the sound of the bellows blown hard.<div eID="gen17209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17210" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lead--</hi>employed to separate the baser metal from the silver, as quicksilver is now used. In other words, the utmost pains have been used to purify Israel in the furnace of affliction, but in vain (<reference osisRef="Jer.5.3">Jr 5:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.7">1Pe 1:7</reference>).<div eID="gen17210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17211" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">consumed of the fire--</hi>In the Chetib, or Hebrew text, the "consumed" is supplied out of the previous "burned." Translating as Rosenmuller, "pant," this will be inadmissible; and the Keri (Hebrew Margin) division of the Hebrew words will have to be read, to get "is consumed of the fire." This is an argument for the translation, "are burned."<div eID="gen17211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17212" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">founder--</hi>the refiner.<div eID="gen17212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17213" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wicked ... not plucked away--</hi>answering to the dross which has no good metal to be separated, the mass being all dross. <div eID="gen17213" type="x-p"/>
entries.e3646074f5d907ae3f8ac8a1539ae3455504d7a7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9740"/><div sID="gen17214" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9740"/><hi type="bold">30. Reprobate--</hi>silver so full of alloy as to be utterly worthless (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.22">Is 1:22</reference>). The Jews were fit only for rejection. <chapter eID="Jer.6"/>

entries.2d8a9ed24b629a98670483d75f667ef19e5bd3c3: <div eID="gen29364" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen29365" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29366" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29366" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29365" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29367" type="x-p"/> Jeremiah, in the spirit of prophecy, seeing the Chaldeans on their march, bids his people set up the usual signals of distress, and spread the general alarm to betake themselves to flight, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.1">Jer 6:1</reference>. Then, by a beautiful allusion to the custom of shepherds moving their flocks to the richest pastures, Jerusalem is singled out as a place devoted to be eaten up or trodden down by the armies of the Chaldeans, who are called up against her, and whose ardor and impatience are so great that the soldiers, when they arrive in the evening, regret they have no more day, and desire to begin the attack without waiting for the light of the morning, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.2-Jer.6.5">Jer 6:2-5</reference>. God is then represented as animating and directing the besiegers against this guilty city, which sinned as incessantly as a fountain flows, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.6">Jer 6:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.7">Jer 6:7</reference>, although warned of the fatal consequence, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.8">Jer 6:8</reference>. He intimates also, by the gleaning of the grapes, that one invasion should carry away the remains of another, till their disobedience, hypocrisy, and other sins should end in their total overthrow, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.9-Jer.6.15">Jer 6:9-15</reference>. And to show that God is clear when he judgeth, he mentions his having in vain admonished and warned them, and calls upon the whole world to witness the equity of his proceedings, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.16-Jer.6.18">Jer 6:16-18</reference>, in punishing this perverse and hypocritical people, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.19">Jer 6:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.20">Jer 6:20</reference>, by the ministry of the cruel Chaldeans, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.21-Jer.6.23">Jer 6:21-23</reference>. Upon this a chorus of Jews is introduced expressing their fears and alarm, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.24">Jer 6:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.25">Jer 6:25</reference>; to which the prophet echoes a response full of sympathy and tenderness, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.26">Jer 6:26</reference>.
